phrases.translation: Ḥâ-Mĩm
phrases.explanation: The surah opens with the disjoint letters Ḥā Mīm. What the letters mean has already been set out at the openings of the surahs that begin the same way, and it is not repeated here. They stand alone as a verse, and the next verse joins them to the Book that is sent down from God, so the letters lead straight into the subject of revelation.

phrases.translation: The revelation of this Book is from Allah—the Almighty, All-Wise
phrases.explanation: What follows rests on a sending down. The Book comes from God rather than from a man, and the two names that close the verse are joined to that act, since the One who sends it is Almighty and All-Wise. Power and wisdom both belong to the sending, and the same opening has already been explained in the surah before this one.

phrases.translation: We only created the heavens and the earth and everything in between for a purpose and an appointed term.
phrases.explanation: The heavens, the earth and everything between them were not made in play. The purpose named is truth, explained as the establishment of truth and justice among created beings. The verse adds an appointed term, a limit known to God alone, at which He will cause the whole of it to pass away and vanish after it had existed. Creation therefore has both a meaning and an end.

phrases.translation: Yet the disbelievers are turning away from what they have been warned about
phrases.explanation: Attention moves from the creation to its hearers. Those who deny God's oneness turn away from the warning given to them, and the turning is described as a habit rather than a single refusal. They take no admonition from what they hear and do not reflect on it, so the lesson never reaches them. The creation supplies the evidence and they decline to look at it.

phrases.translation: Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Have you considered whatever ˹idols˺ you invoke besides Allah? Show me what they have created on earth!
phrases.explanation: The idolaters are asked about the gods they call on. They must show anything those gods created, and the point is that the reply is empty. The whole earth is God's making, brought out of nothing without any prior model, while the idols named have made nothing at all. The challenge exposes the absence of any ground for worshipping them.

phrases.translation: Or do they have a share in ˹the creation of˺ the heavens?
phrases.explanation: The second question widens the test. If the idols did not create anything on earth, do they share the heavens with God? A share would be a ground for worship, and the verse denies that any exists. The heavens are named because they are the greater part of creation and beyond the reach of any claim the idolaters could make. God alone made them, to the exclusion of all else.

phrases.translation: Bring me a scripture ˹revealed˺ before this ˹Quran˺ or a shred of knowledge, if what you say is true.”
phrases.explanation: The third demand asks for evidence. They are told to produce a book from before this one, or a remnant of knowledge supporting what they say about their gods. The word is read in several ways, as a leftover of knowledge, a special knowledge, a line drawn in the earth, or a report handed down, and the form taken as a remnant is the one preferred. Whatever the reading, the claim needs proof, and none is offered.

phrases.translation: And who could be more astray than those who call upon others besides Allah—
phrases.explanation: Who could be further from the road than a person who calls on something other than God? The answer is left to the hearer, since the case is plain. The gods invoked are stone or wood, and the verse notes that they will not answer until the Day of Resurrection. The delay is not a pause before an answer, it is the absence of any answer at all.

phrases.translation: ˹others˺ that cannot respond to them until the Day of Judgment, and are ˹even˺ unaware of their calls
phrases.explanation: Their heedlessness is described in human terms, because they neither hear nor speak nor understand. They are unaware of the calls made to them, as a heedless person is unaware of what is said in his presence. The verse treats the comparison as a rebuke: the idolaters forsake the One from whom every favour comes and call instead on what understands nothing. The plural wording is used because their worshippers likened them to kings attended by servants.

phrases.translation: And when ˹such˺ people will be gathered together, those ˹gods˺ will be their enemies
phrases.explanation: On the Day of Resurrection the gods and the people who served them are gathered together, and the relation between them is reversed. What was called upon as a patron becomes an enemy, and the enmity is public rather than private. The verse sets the scene for the disowning that follows, since the same assembly that honoured them in the world now hears them speak against their worshippers.

phrases.translation: and will disown their worship
phrases.explanation: The gods deny that they were worshipped and refuse the service offered to them. They say that they never commanded it and were not aware of it, and they disavow their worshippers before their Lord. The verse makes the idols witnesses against those who invoked them, which leaves the worshippers with no defence. The very things they trusted to intercede for them are the first to renounce them.

phrases.translation: Whenever Our clear revelations are recited to them, the disbelievers say of the truth when it has come to them,
phrases.explanation: The moment of recitation is described. The verses are called clear proofs, plain and luminous in themselves, so the fault cannot lie in their obscurity. The disbelievers speak about the truth as soon as it reaches them, and they speak before they have considered it. The recitation comes first in the sentence and the reaction after it, so the reaction answers something already clear.

phrases.translation: “This is pure magic.”
phrases.explanation: Their answer names the Book as sorcery, a deception that takes hold of the hearts of those who hear it. The description is meant as an accusation, yet it grants the recitation a power to move people that they cannot explain otherwise. The verse adds that the magic is manifest, meaning that anyone who considers it attentively can see what it is. The label is a refusal to engage rather than a judgement formed from the text.

phrases.translation: Or do they say, “He has fabricated this ˹Quran˺!”? Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “If I have done so, then there is nothing whatsoever you can do to save me from Allah.
phrases.explanation: The charge is that the Prophet invented the Book himself. The answer does not begin by denying it but by showing what would follow if it were true: if he had invented a lie against God, none of his accusers could shield him from the punishment that would fall on him. Their inability to help him is the point, since they have no power against God either way. The verse turns their accusation into a proof of their weakness.

phrases.translation: He knows best what ˹slurs˺ you indulge about it.
phrases.explanation: God knows what they say among themselves about the Book, and the verse leaves that knowledge with Him. One report explains the words as referring to the talk they exchange about the revelation. The sentence is a warning rather than a threat, since it places their private conversation in plain view. What they think is hidden is recorded, and the witness named in the next phrase is the One who records it.

phrases.translation: Sufficient is He as a Witness between you and me. And He is the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”
phrases.explanation: God is enough as a witness between the Prophet and his people. The witness is needed because each side denies the other's account, and the verse settles the dispute by naming the One who sees both. The two names that follow close the sentence with mercy, since the offer of forgiveness remains open to any who turn back from denial. The verse therefore ends on pardon after a warning.

phrases.translation: Say, “I am not the first messenger ever sent,
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to say that he is no novelty among the messengers. Messengers came before him to peoples before his own, so the coming of a warner is not a strange event and the message is not without precedent. The word used is explained as meaning the first of a kind, and the verse denies that he is the first. The objection that the message is unheard of is therefore answered from history.

phrases.translation: nor do I know what will happen to me or you.
phrases.explanation: The clause was understood in more than one way. One view takes it as referring to the next life, and says it was later clarified when God told the Prophet of his forgiveness and of the believers' reward. Another view, preferred as closer to the passage, takes it as referring to this world, whether he would be killed or driven out and whether his people would believe. God then informed him of both outcomes.

phrases.translation: I only follow what is revealed to me. And I am only sent with a clear warning.”
phrases.explanation: The Prophet states his own position plainly. In what he commands and in what he does, he follows only what is revealed to him, so the message is not his own invention. He is a warner, and the warning is described as clear, since he has made it plain and shown the way of deliverance openly. The verse closes the answer to the charge of fabrication by pointing to the revelation behind him.

phrases.translation: Ask ˹them, O Prophet˺, “Consider if this ˹Quran˺ is ˹truly˺ from Allah and you deny it,
phrases.explanation: The address returns to the charge of sorcery. The idolaters are asked to consider the case in which the Book really is from God and they are the ones rejecting it. The question is not answered for them, since the point is to make them weigh what they are denying. Everything in the surah up to this point has been building the argument, and the verse states it in one sentence.

phrases.translation: and a witness from the Children of Israel attests to it and then believes, whereas you act arrogantly.
phrases.explanation: A witness from among the Israelites is said to testify to something like the Book and then believe. One report takes the witness as Moses, who confirmed a scripture resembling this one, so the Torah answers the Qur'an and Moses answers Muhammad, while these people refuse. Many reports name a Jewish scholar of Medina who testified to the Prophet and was rejected by his own people. Both readings agree that belief came from one side and arrogance from the other.

phrases.translation: Surely Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.”
phrases.explanation: The verse closes with a statement about guidance. God does not guide the wrongdoing people, meaning those who have wronged themselves by disbelief and have brought down wrath on themselves. Their arrogance is not a small fault, since it placed them among those who refuse the very thing that would have saved them. The sentence is a verdict on the refusal described before it, not a comment on their chances.

phrases.translation: The disbelievers say of the believers, “Had it been ˹something˺ good, they would not have beaten us to it.”
phrases.explanation: The disbelievers are heard speaking about those who believed. Their argument is that if the message had been any good, the believers would not have reached it before them, since they counted themselves the stronger and the more worthy. One report places the words among the leaders of the Quraysh who measured truth by precedence among tribes. Another places them among the Jews speaking of a believer from their own number. In both cases the measure is status rather than evidence.

phrases.translation: Now since they reject its guidance, they will say, “˹This is˺ an ancient fabrication!”
phrases.explanation: Their rejection produces a second sentence. Because they found no guidance in it, they call it an ancient fabrication, the tales of former peoples written down and recited morning and evening. The verse shows the order of the two statements, denial first and then the label that makes denial respectable. Nothing in the accusation explains why the Book fails, it only names where they suppose it came from. The next verse answers that with the Book of Moses.

phrases.translation: And before this ˹Quran˺ the Book of Moses was ˹revealed as˺ a guide and mercy.
phrases.explanation: This reaches back before the Qur'an. The Book of Moses was given as a guide by which the Israelites were directed and as a mercy sent down to them. The sentence is left short because its sense is already complete, and the next clause supplies the pairing. Precedent is the point: a scripture that guides and shows mercy is not a new kind of event, and the people who received the earlier one are in no position to deny this one.

phrases.translation: And this Book is a confirmation, in the Arabic tongue,
phrases.explanation: The Book is described as confirming what came before it, and as coming in an Arabic tongue. The phrase is read as a description of the Book itself, so the confirmation is carried in Arabic speech addressed to the people who hear it. The grammar of the clause is discussed at length, and one early reading adds the words that it confirms what preceded it. The sense is that the confirmation reaches its hearers in their own language.

phrases.translation: to warn those who do wrong, and as good news to those who do good
phrases.explanation: The purposes are named as warning and good news. The warning is for those who have wronged themselves by disbelief and by worshipping what is not God, and the good news is for those who obeyed and did well. The reciters read the verb either as you may warn, addressing the Prophet, or as the Book may warn, and both readings are accepted. The verse closes by joining the two audiences that the surah keeps in view.

phrases.translation: Surely those who say, “Our Lord is Allah,” and then remain steadfast—
phrases.explanation: The saved are named by what they say and by what they do after saying it. They declare that their Lord is God, the One besides whom there is no god, and then remain steadfast on that declaration. Steadfastness is explained as keeping it unmixed with any partner and as obeying God in what He commands and forbids. The word covers both the belief and the life that follows from it.

phrases.translation: there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve
phrases.explanation: Two fears are removed. They will not be seized by the terror of the Day of Resurrection and its horrors, and they will not grieve over what they left behind in the world after death. The verse mentions both because people fear what is coming and mourn what is gone, and it denies each in turn. The promise is stated in the negative, which is how security too large to be measured is often described.

phrases.translation: It is they who will be the residents of Paradise, staying there forever, as a reward for what they used to do
phrases.explanation: Their destination is named. Those who made the declaration and held to it are the people of Paradise and its inhabitants, dwelling there forever without end. The last clause gives the reason as a recompense from God for the good deeds they performed in the world. The reward is called a repayment, which keeps the verse from suggesting that the dwelling was owed to them, since it is God who grants it.

phrases.translation: We have commanded people to honour their parents.
phrases.explanation: The surah turns from the adversaries of the Book to a duty owed at home. People are commanded to treat their parents well, and the goodness is explained as covering their lifetime and what comes after their death. Two readings of the word are reported, one naming the goodness itself and the other naming the doing of it, and both are accepted because their meanings are close. The command belongs to the upright life the Book teaches.

phrases.translation: Their mothers bore them in hardship and delivered them in hardship. Their ˹period of˺ bearing and weaning is thirty months.
phrases.explanation: The reason for the duty is then given. The mother carried the child in discomfort and gave birth in discomfort, and the period of carrying and weaning together comes to thirty months. The two words for hardship are read with different vowels and carry the same sense of difficulty. The verse sets out what the parents underwent before it asks for anything in return, so the command rests on a debt already owed rather than on sentiment.

phrases.translation: In time, when the child reaches their prime at the age of forty, they pray, “My Lord! Inspire me to ˹always˺ be thankful for Your favours which You blessed me and my parents with, and to do good deeds that please You. And instil righteousness in my offspring.
phrases.explanation: At full strength and forty years the person prays. Full strength is placed at thirty-three by some and at puberty by others, and the earlier figure is preferred because forty follows it more naturally. At forty the proof against a person is complete. The prayer asks to be helped to thank God for the favour of guidance, for deeds that please Him, and for offspring made righteous. One report ties the verse to a man of the Companions.

phrases.translation: I truly repent to You, and I truly submit ˹to Your Will˺.”
phrases.explanation: The prayer ends with two declarations. The speaker turns to God in repentance from the sins of his earlier days, and he places himself among those who submit, surrendering to God's command and prohibition and accepting His judgement. The two together describe a life that has turned and then stayed turned. The verse closes on that note, so the gratitude and the good deeds it asks for are framed as the fruit of repentance rather than as a claim.

phrases.translation: It is from these ˹people˺ that We will accept the good they did, and overlook their misdeeds—
phrases.explanation: Those who speak this way are the ones from whom God accepts the best of what they did and passes over their evil deeds. The acceptance is explained as reward for the good and forgiveness for the bad, so that a life mixed with faults is not thrown away. One report describes deeds being weighed against one another and a remaining good deed being enlarged in the Garden. The verse measures such people by their best rather than their worst.

phrases.translation: along with the residents of Paradise, ˹in fulfilment of˺ the true promise they have been given
phrases.explanation: Their destination is named with the rest of the people of Paradise, since the promise made to them in the world is true and will be fulfilled. The word promise is put in a form that stresses its truthfulness, and the reciters read the verbs either as a report about God or as God speaking of Himself, both being correct. The verse closes the account of the grateful and the dutiful by placing them among the inhabitants of the Garden.

phrases.translation: But some scold their parents, “Enough with you! Are you warning me that I will be brought forth ˹from the grave˺, while many generations had already perished before me ˹for good˺?”
phrases.explanation: A portrait is given of a man who answers his parents with contempt. They call him to believe that God will raise the dead, and he rejects the call and asks whether they are really promising that he will be brought out of his grave. He adds that generations have passed before him and none returned, which he takes as proof. The scene sets obstinacy beside the counsel of parents who want only his good.

phrases.translation: The parents cry to Allah for help, ˹and warn their child,˺ “Pity you. Have faith! Surely Allah’s promise is true.”
phrases.explanation: The parents do not answer insult with insult. They call on God for help, and they urge their son to believe, warning him that the promise of God is true. Their plea is short and it rests entirely on the truth of that promise rather than on their authority as parents. The verse gives them the patience that the surah has just praised in the dutiful son.

phrases.translation: But the deniers insist, “This is nothing but ancient fables.”
phrases.explanation: His reply is the same label the surah has already reported from the deniers. He calls the warning ancient fables, the stories of former peoples written down and handed on, and with that he dismisses the resurrection and the judgement. The verse ends on that refusal, and the next verse announces where such a person stands. The exchange is left without further argument, since the man has stopped listening.

phrases.translation: These are the ones against whom the fate of earlier communities of jinn and humans has been justified,
phrases.explanation: Such a man is placed in a line. The sentence pronounced against earlier communities of jinn and humankind, who denied the messengers and turned away from God's command, is now settled against him as well. The phrase speaks of a word already proven true, so his case is not a fresh judgement but the same one reached again. The mention of jinn alongside humans widens the company of the condemned.

phrases.translation: ˹for˺ they were truly losers
phrases.explanation: The last clause names the outcome. They were losers because they sold guidance for error and happiness for punishment, as one report puts it, and the loss lies in the exchange they made. The verse states the verdict without describing the Fire, since the surah has already described it. It closes the account of the man who insulted his parents and leaves him among those who lost by their own trade.

phrases.translation: Each ˹of the two groups˺ will be ranked according to what they have done
phrases.explanation: Both groups are given ranks. The believers who honoured their parents and the disbelievers who scorned them each have a station with God on the Day of Resurrection, measured by what they did in the world. One report notes that the ranks of the Fire descend while the ranks of the Garden ascend, so the two directions are opposite. Each person is placed where his own work puts him.

phrases.translation: so He may fully reward all. And none will be wronged
phrases.explanation: The purpose is that every deed be repaid in full. The doer of good receives what God has promised, and the doer of evil receives what his sin deserves, and the verse denies that anyone will be wronged in the settlement. No one is punished for what he did not do, and no one is robbed of the reward of what he did. The two denials together guarantee that the ranks just described are just.

phrases.translation: ˹Watch for˺ the Day ˹when˺ the disbelievers will be exposed to the Fire.
phrases.explanation: The scene shifts to the day of reckoning. The disbelievers are brought before the Fire and made to stand at its edge, so that what they denied is now in front of them. The verse gives no dialogue yet, only the exposure itself, which is the first part of the punishment. The placement is deliberate, since everything they are about to hear is spoken from that position.

phrases.translation: ˹They will be told,˺ “You ˹already˺ exhausted your ˹share of˺ pleasures during your worldly life, and ˹fully˺ enjoyed them.
phrases.explanation: The charge is that they took their share of good things in the world and used it up. Their pleasures were not forbidden to them, but they were consumed here and nothing was kept for the life to come. One report says that some peoples lose their good deeds this way, and a saying attributed to a Companion advises sparing them. The verse treats enjoyment as a spending that leaves no balance.

phrases.translation: So Today you will be rewarded with the torment of disgrace for your arrogance throughout the land with no right,
phrases.explanation: The recompense matches their conduct. They are paid with a punishment that humiliates them, because in the world they were arrogant on the earth without any right to be. Their arrogance is explained as refusing to worship God alone and to submit to what He commanded and forbade, and the verse adds that no permission had been given for it. The humbling answers the height they claimed.

phrases.translation: and for your rebelliousness.”
phrases.explanation: The last words name their defiance. They transgressed God's obedience and broke His command, and that is the second charge added to arrogance. The two together describe a person who set himself above the law and then stepped over it. The verse closes the address and leaves the sentence complete, with the reason stated twice for the same offence.

phrases.translation: And remember the brother of ’Ȃd, when he warned his people, who inhabited the sand-hills—
phrases.explanation: The surah turns to a warners' precedent. The Prophet is told to remember Hūd, the brother of the tribe of ʿĀd, who was sent to people living among the sand-hills. The word for those hills is explained as long ridges of sand that never rise into mountains, and reports place them in several regions, from a mountain in Syria to a valley between Oman and Mahra. What matters is the people and the warning, not the location.

phrases.translation: there were certainly warners before and after him—
phrases.explanation: The verse notes that warners had come before Hūd and after him, so his mission was one link in a long chain rather than an isolated event. One early reading makes the point explicitly, that the messengers passed away with their warnings. The hearers in Mecca are therefore being told that their own messenger stands where earlier warners stood, and that the pattern is a familiar one.

phrases.translation: ˹saying,˺ “Worship none but Allah. I truly fear for you the torment of a tremendous day.”
phrases.explanation: The content of the warning is stated in one sentence. They are to worship God alone, giving Him no partner, and Hūd tells them that he fears for them the punishment of a tremendous day. The day is explained as the Day of Resurrection, whose terror is great. The verse leaves the fear on the warner's side, since he is not threatening them from himself but reporting what he knows will come.

phrases.translation: They argued, “Have you come to turn us away from our gods?
phrases.explanation: The reply of the people is a question. They ask whether Hūd has come to turn them from their gods toward what he calls them to, and the phrasing shows that they understand his message as a demand to abandon their worship. They do not ask whether their gods are true. The verse records the question without comment, since the next sentence shows what they wanted instead of an answer.

phrases.translation: Bring us then whatever you threaten us with, if what you say is true.”
phrases.explanation: Their demand is for the punishment itself. If what Hūd says is true, let him bring the threat down on them at once, and they treat the delay as a weakness in his case. The verse shows that they had no patience for a warning whose time is not theirs to set. Their challenge is answered in the next two verses, and it is answered in the form they asked for.

phrases.translation: He responded, “The knowledge ˹of its time˺ is only with Allah.
phrases.explanation: Hūd answers the challenge by naming where the knowledge belongs. The time of the punishment is with God, and he knows of it only what he has been taught. A messenger who announced the hour himself would be claiming what belongs to his Lord, and the verse keeps that distinction firm. The answer also removes the test they proposed, since the date was never his to give.

phrases.translation: I only convey to you what I have been sent with. But I can see that you are a people acting ignorantly.”
phrases.explanation: His task is then stated. He conveys what he was sent with and nothing more, so the warning is delivered without a schedule attached. He adds that he sees a people acting ignorantly, and the ignorance is explained as not knowing where their own good lies. They cannot see the harm in worshipping something other than God, nor the folly of demanding the punishment before its time.

phrases.translation: Then when they saw the torment as a ˹dense˺ cloud approaching their valleys, they said ˹happily˺, “This is a cloud bringing us rain.”
phrases.explanation: The scene is described from the ground. The punishment appears as a dark mass stretched across the sky and moving toward their valleys, and the people read it as the rain they had been waiting for. Their words show relief rather than fear, since rain meant life for a people whose water had been withheld. The verse lets them mistake the very thing they asked for, which is the sharpest part of the account.

phrases.translation: ˹But Hûd replied,˺ “No, it is what you sought to hasten: a ˹fierce˺ wind carrying a painful punishment!”
phrases.explanation: Hūd corrects them at once. It is not rain but the thing they demanded when they challenged him to bring the threat, a wind carrying a painful punishment. The verse names the wind because that is what the cloud held. Their demand to hasten the punishment is answered by its arrival, and the answer needs no argument. The next verse reports what the wind did.

phrases.translation: It destroyed everything by the command of its Lord, leaving nothing visible except their ruins.
phrases.explanation: The wind did what it was sent to do. It destroyed everything by its Lord's command, and the destruction is explained as one thing cast upon another until nothing stood. The verse limits the ruin to what the wind was sent for, since Hūd and those who believed with him were not touched. What remained were the dwellings, empty shells that showed where the people had lived, and one report says the wind itself was no wider than a ring.

phrases.translation: This is how We reward the wicked people
phrases.explanation: The verse draws the lesson out of the story. Just as ʿĀd were recompensed for their denial with destruction in this world, so are the criminals of every later generation repaid. The punishment is not a single event in the past but a pattern in God's dealing with those who persist in error and set themselves against their Lord. The sentence is brief because the example has already made the case.

phrases.translation: Indeed, We had established them in a way We have not established you ˹Meccans˺.
phrases.explanation: The address turns to the people of Mecca and sets the destroyed tribe before them. ʿĀd had been given a footing in the world that the Meccans were never given, with abundance of possessions, greater stature and bodily strength. The verse does not say the Meccans were weak, only that their power was less. The comparison removes any excuse they might draw from their own standing, since those who were stronger still perished.

phrases.translation: And We gave them hearing, sight, and intellect.
phrases.explanation: The verse lists what was given besides power. They had hearing to hear their Lord's admonitions, eyes to see His proofs, and hearts to understand what would profit them. The three are named in the order of how a person receives knowledge, from hearing to sight to understanding. The gifts are described as instruments, which sets up the charge that follows, since they were given to be used and not merely possessed.

phrases.translation: But neither their hearing, sight, nor intellect were of any benefit to them whatsoever, since they persisted in denying Allah’s signs. And ˹so˺ they were overwhelmed by what they used to ridicule
phrases.explanation: None of it helped them, and the reason is given. They did not use these faculties for the purpose they were given, and turned them instead toward what brought God's displeasure. Since they kept denying the signs and rejecting the messengers, the very thing they mocked came back on them and overwhelmed them. The verse closes with a warning to the Meccans that the same end waits for the same conduct.

phrases.translation: We certainly destroyed the societies around you
phrases.explanation: The Meccans are told to look at their surroundings. Towns that lay around their own had been destroyed, among them the settlements of Thamūd, the cities of the plain and the people of Ma'rib, and their dwellings were left as ruins fallen on their roofs. The verse treats the ruins as evidence within reach, not as a story from a distant age. The destruction came after warning, not in place of it.

phrases.translation: after having varied the signs so perhaps they would return ˹to the Right Path˺
phrases.explanation: The signs were varied before the end came. God admonished them with every kind of admonition and made the proofs clear, so that the warning could not be missed or called obscure. The purpose is stated as their return, meaning that they might turn back from the disbelief they persisted in. The sentence leaves unsaid what happened next, since the sense already carries it: they refused and the punishment came.

phrases.translation: Why then did those ˹idols˺ they took as gods—hoping to get closer ˹to Him˺—not come to their aid?
phrases.explanation: The idolaters of every time are asked the same thing. If the gods they took as a means of drawing near to God had any power, they would have come to the aid of the peoples destroyed before them. The verse names the hope behind the worship, that the idols would bring them closer, and then tests it against what actually happened. The silence of the idols is the answer.

phrases.translation: Instead, they failed them. That is ˹the result of˺ their lies and their fabrications
phrases.explanation: The idols did not help, they failed the people who trusted them. They abandoned their worshippers and went their own way, since stones and metal were untouched by what struck the towns while those who called on them perished. The verse calls this the working out of their lie, the claim that these were gods able to intercede. Both readings of the last word describe the same failure.

phrases.translation: ˹Remember, O Prophet,˺ when We sent a group of jinn your way to listen to the Quran.
phrases.explanation: The verse turns to an event the Prophet is told to remember. A company of jinn was directed toward him so that they would hear the Qur'an, and the reports describe them coming upon him while he recited at dawn in a valley near Mecca. One account ties their search to the shooting stars that guarded the sky after his sending. Whether he knew of them at the time is disputed, and one report says God informed him afterwards.

phrases.translation: Then, upon hearing it, they said ˹to one another˺, “Listen quietly!”
phrases.explanation: Their first exchange is a command to be quiet. They said it to one another so that nothing would distract them from listening, and the reports note that people cannot understand what they do not attend to. The verse gives the scene its small human detail, a group falling silent to catch what is being recited. Their listening is deliberate, which makes what follows a considered response rather than an accident.

phrases.translation: Then when it was over, they returned to their fellow jinn as warners
phrases.explanation: When the recitation ended they went back to their own people as warners. They did not keep what they had heard, and they did not treat the event as a curiosity, they carried the warning home. The verse makes them messengers to their kind, and the reports add that the Prophet sent them for that purpose. Their return prepares for the speech they make in the next verses, where they explain what they heard.

phrases.translation: They declared, “O our fellow jinn! We have truly heard a scripture revealed after Moses, confirming what came before it.
phrases.explanation: The jinn speak to their own people. They announce what they heard, a Book sent down after the Book of Moses that confirms the scriptures before it. The mention of Moses places the new revelation in the line the jinn already knew, and their testimony is that it agrees with what came earlier rather than cancelling it. The verse has them address their people as a community, since the warning is meant for all of them.

phrases.translation: It guides to the truth and the Straight Way
phrases.explanation: The Book is then described by what it does. It guides to the truth, meaning to what is right and to what earns God's pleasure, and to a straight path in which there is no crookedness. The path is explained as Islam, the way of submission. The two phrases move from the destination to the road, so that the jinn commend both the goal and the manner of reaching it.

phrases.translation: O our fellow jinn! Respond to the caller of Allah and believe in him,
phrases.explanation: Their call to their people is direct. They ask them to answer the one who calls to God, meaning the Prophet, in what he calls them to of obedience, and to believe in him and in what he brought of command and prohibition. The jinn do not present the message as their own idea but as a summons that has reached them and now reaches their people. The invitation is put before the warning that follows.

phrases.translation: He will forgive your sins and protect you from a painful punishment
phrases.explanation: The promise attached to belief is stated plainly. God will forgive them a portion of their sins and will not disgrace them for it in the Hereafter, and He will save them from a painful punishment. The condition is repentance and the turn from disbelief to belief. The verse holds out both pardon and protection, and it addresses a people who had heard the Book only recently and were asked to answer at once.

phrases.translation: And whoever does not respond to the caller of Allah will have no escape on earth,
phrases.explanation: The warning turns to those who refuse. No one who declines the summons can escape by fleeing, since wherever he goes on the earth he remains within God's dominion and within His grasp. The verse removes the hope that distance might serve as protection. The earth is named because it is the widest place a person can go, and even there the refusal buys nothing.

phrases.translation: nor will they have any protectors against Him.
phrases.explanation: Nor will there be protectors besides God. No helper can shield the one who refuses when his Lord punishes him for his denial, and the verse denies the assistance that people expect from patrons. The two clauses together close every route out, the road and the ally. What remains is the person alone with the consequence of his own answer.

phrases.translation: It is they who are clearly astray.”
phrases.explanation: The verdict is that such people are clearly astray. Their error is not hidden or doubtful, since the summons was plain and they turned from it, taking a way that is not straight. The verse adds that the error is manifest to anyone who reflects on it. It closes the speech of the jinn and leaves their people with the choice the whole surah has been presenting.

phrases.translation: Do they not realize that Allah, Who created the heavens and the earth and did not tire in creating them, is able to give life to the dead?
phrases.explanation: The question is put to those who deny the raising of the dead. They are asked to look at the making of the heavens and the earth, which God brought out of nothing, and to notice that the work did not weary Him. If creating on that scale cost Him no fatigue, giving life to the dead cannot be beyond Him. The argument moves from the greater to the lesser, and it also answers the man who scoffed at the promise in the previous verses.

phrases.translation: Yes ˹indeed˺! He is certainly Most Capable of everything
phrases.explanation: The answer follows in the affirmative. Yes, He is able to do all things, and the verse states it as a conclusion rather than a hope. The word for capable is read in more than one form by the reciters, all of them agreeing on the sense. The sentence closes the argument by naming the attribute that makes the resurrection possible, so that the denial is left with nothing to stand on.

phrases.translation: And on the Day the disbelievers will be exposed to the Fire, ˹they will be asked,˺ “Is this ˹Hereafter˺ not the truth?”
phrases.explanation: The scene returns to the Fire. Those who denied the raising of the dead are brought before it and asked whether this, the punishment they used to reject, is not the truth. The question is a rebuke rather than a request for information, since the answer is already visible to them. The verse puts them in the position they refused in the world, where the truth had to be taken on trust.

phrases.translation: They will cry, “Absolutely, by our Lord!” It will be said, “Then taste the punishment for your disbelief.”
phrases.explanation: They answer at once and swear by their Lord that it is true. The confession comes too late to change anything, since it is made when the proof is in front of them and not when faith was still possible. The command that follows tells them to taste the punishment for their disbelief. The verse ends with the acknowledgement they withheld, and it shows that the withholding was the offence.

phrases.translation: So endure patiently, as did the Messengers of Firm Resolve. And do not ˹seek to˺ hasten ˹the torment˺ for the deniers.
phrases.explanation: The surah closes with a command to the Prophet. He is to endure what his people inflict on him, as the messengers of firm resolve endured before him, those who were tested and only grew in zeal. The verse names no messenger here, and the reports list Noah, Abraham and Moses among them, with one view holding that every messenger possessed resolve. He is also told not to ask that the punishment be hastened, since it will come at its appointed time.

phrases.translation: On the Day they see what they have been threatened with, it will be as if they had only stayed ˹in this world˺ for an hour of a day.
phrases.explanation: The delay is measured from the other side. On the day they see what they were promised, the whole span of their life in the world will seem to them no more than an hour of a day. The terror of what descends makes them forget the years and months they spent there. The verse uses their own sense of time to show how short the period of denial was, and how little it bought.

phrases.translation: ˹This is˺ a ˹sufficient˺ warning! Then, will anyone be destroyed except the rebellious people
phrases.explanation: The last words are a proclamation, and the closing question repeats the point. The Qur'an and its admonition are enough for anyone who reflects, and when the punishment falls it destroys only the rebellious, those who turned against God's command and left His obedience. One report adds that none perishes except the one who turns his back on the faith. The surah ends with the Book and the choice it sets before its hearers.
